tips.title: J'ai mal au, à la, aux
tips.body: *À* contracts with the article: *j'ai mal **au** ventre*, ***à la** tête*, ***aux** dents*. Never *à le* or *à les*, which do not exist in French.

tips.title: Reflexive verbs always take être
tips.body: *Je **me suis** cassé le bras*, never *j'ai me cassé*. Every reflexive verb forms the perfect with **être**, without exception.

tips.title: Grave means serious
tips.body: *Ce n'est pas grave* means *it is not serious*. It has nothing to do with the English noun *a grave*, which is *une tombe*.

tips.title: One phrase covers every ache
tips.body: Learn **avoir mal à** once and the whole topic opens up, because only the article changes: *au dos*, *à la tête*, *aux dents*. Learn each body part **with its article** and the contraction to *au* or *aux* then happens automatically.

steps.title: Saying what hurts
steps.body: The phrase to know cold is **avoir mal à** — literally *to have pain at*. The **à** joins to the article in front of the body part, and the contraction depends on the gender: - masculine: **au** — *j'ai mal **au** dos* - feminine: **à la** — *j'ai mal **à la** tête* - before a vowel: **à l'** — *j'ai mal à l'estomac* - plural: **aux** — *j'ai mal **aux** dents* *À le* and *à les* are never written. They always contract. So you have to learn each body part **with its article**, exactly as with any other noun. *La main* is feminine even though it does not look it.

visuals.fallback: la tête — head; le dos — back; le ventre — stomach; la gorge — throat; la jambe — leg; le bras — arm; la main — hand; le pied — foot; les dents — teeth; la cheville — ankle.

props.title: avoir mal à + the body part

visuals.alt: A table showing how à contracts with each article before a body part

check.solution: *Le ventre* is masculine and singular, so *à + le* contracts to **au**.

steps.title: Being ill
steps.body:
Beyond aches, you need the words for actually being unwell, and the places you go.

Two patterns worth separating:

- **être** + adjective: *je suis malade*, *je suis fatigué*.
- **avoir** + noun: *j'ai un rhume*, *j'ai la grippe*, *j'ai de la fièvre*.

Notice *j'ai **de la** fièvre* — a partitive, because it is an unspecified amount of it.

And one false friend that catches people in the reading paper: **une ordonnance** is a *prescription*, not an order or an ordinance. **Grave** means *serious* — *ce n'est pas grave*. It has nothing to do with the English noun *a grave*, which is *une tombe*.

visuals.fallback: un rhume — a cold; la grippe — flu; la fièvre — a temperature; malade — ill; une ordonnance — a prescription; un médicament — medicine; le médecin — the doctor; la pharmacie — the chemist's; les urgences — A and E; tousser — to cough.

check.solution: A classic false friend: **une ordonnance** is a *prescription*. The reading paper sets these deliberately.

steps.title: The perfect tense, briefly
steps.body:
You met the perfect tense in Year 9. It has two parts: an **auxiliary** in the present, then a **past participle**.

Most verbs take **avoir**: *j'ai mangé*, *j'ai fait*, *j'ai eu*.

A small group of movement verbs take **être**, and with those the past participle **agrees with the subject**: *je suis allé*, and a girl writes *je suis allée*; *nous sommes tombés*.

Past participles are formed from the infinitive:

- *-er* → **-é**: *tomber* → *tombé*
- *-ir* → **-i**: *finir* → *fini*
- *-re* → **-u**: *vendre* → *vendu*

Irregulars have to be learnt: *faire* → **fait**, *avoir* → **eu**, *être* → **été**, *prendre* → **pris**, *voir* → **vu**.

visuals.alt: A table of the three past participle endings and some irregular participles

steps.text: *Tomber* is a movement verb, so the auxiliary is **être**: *elle est…*
The *-er* participle is *tombé*
With *être* the participle agrees with *elle*: *tombée*
*Elle est tombée.* Compare *manger*, which takes **avoir**: *elle a mangé*
steps.note: after *avoir* the participle never agrees with the subject

check.prompt: What is the past participle of **tomber**?
check.solution: *Tomber* is an *-er* verb, so the participle ends **-é**: *tombé*.

steps.title: Reflexive verbs in the perfect: always être
steps.body:
Here is the rule this whole topic turns on.

**Every reflexive verb takes être in the perfect.** No exceptions, no list to learn.

The order is: subject, **reflexive pronoun**, **être**, past participle.

*Je **me suis** couché.* *Elle **s'est** blessée.* *Nous **nous sommes** reposés.*

Because it is *être*, the participle normally **agrees with the subject**:

- a boy: *je me suis couché*
- a girl: *je me suis couché**e***
- a mixed or male group: *ils se sont couché**s***
- a female group: *elles se sont couché**es***

The pronoun shortens before the vowel of *est* and *es*: *il **s'est**…*, *tu **t'es**…*

The commonest mistake is using *avoir*: *j'ai me couché* is not French. If it is reflexive, it is **être**.

visuals.alt: A table of se blesser in the perfect tense, showing the reflexive pronoun, the être auxiliary and the agreeing past participle

steps.text: Start with the subject and its pronoun: *elle **se**…*
Add **être** in the present, shortening the pronoun: *elle **s'est**…*
steps.note: Not *elle s'a* — reflexives never take avoir

steps.text: Add the participle: *elle s'est **blessé**…*
Agree it with the subject: *elle s'est **blessée***
steps.note: One -e, because elle is feminine singular

check.prompt: Which is correct for a girl?
check.solution: Reflexives take **être**, and the participle agrees with the subject, so a girl adds **-e**: *je me suis reposée*.

steps.title: Accidents
steps.body:
Most accident verbs are reflexive, which is why they sit here.

- **se casser** — to break (a bone): *je me suis cassé le bras*
- **se blesser** — to injure oneself: *elle s'est blessée*
- **se faire mal** — to hurt oneself: *je me suis fait mal*
- **tomber** — to fall: *je suis tombé* (not reflexive, but still **être**)
- **glisser** — to slip: *j'ai glissé* (takes **avoir**)

One difference from English worth noticing: French says **the** part, not *my* part. *Je me suis cassé **la** jambe* — the reflexive pronoun already tells you whose leg it is, so *ma jambe* is redundant and wrong.

visuals.fallback: se casser — to break a bone; se blesser — to injure oneself; se faire mal — to hurt oneself; tomber — to fall; glisser — to slip; une blessure — an injury; un accident — an accident; grave — serious.

visuals.problem: Build: *I broke my arm.* (you are a boy)

steps.text: *Se casser* is reflexive, so the perfect takes **être**: *je me suis…*
The participle is *cassé*
French says **the** arm, not *my*: *le bras*
steps.note: **me** already says whose arm it is

steps.text: *Je me suis cassé le bras.*

check.solution: **Je suis tombé.** *Tomber* takes **être**, and the participle agrees with the subject.

steps.title: At the doctor's
steps.body:
A role play at the doctor's or the chemist's comes up regularly, and it runs on a small set of phrases. Learn them as whole units rather than word by word.

The doctor uses **vous**, so the pronoun goes before the infinitive: *je vais **vous** donner…*

steps.text: *Qu'est-ce qui ne va pas ?* — What's wrong?
*J'ai mal à la gorge et j'ai de la fièvre depuis deux jours.* — I've had a sore throat and a temperature for two days
*Depuis* + present means *for* or *since*, and French keeps the **present** where English uses a past
steps.note: *J'ai mal depuis deux jours* — I **have had** it for two days

steps.text: *Je vais vous donner une ordonnance. Prenez ce médicament trois fois par jour.*
*Merci, docteur. Au revoir.*

check.prompt: *J'ai mal à la tête depuis trois jours* means:
check.solution: **Depuis** + the present tense means the situation started in the past and is **still going on**, so English uses *have had*. This mismatch is a favourite of the reading paper.

options: I had a headache three days ago
I had a headache for three days

steps.title: Your turn: the words you need cold
steps.body:
Everything in this topic rests on the body parts with their articles and the accident verbs. Cover the English, say each one, and use the speaker to check.

As you go, say the whole phrase rather than the bare noun: not *tête* but ***j'ai mal à la tête***. The article and the contraction are where the marks are, and learning them apart from the noun means learning them twice.

visuals.fallback: Cover the English: la tête, le dos, le ventre, la gorge, la jambe, le bras, se casser, se blesser, se faire mal, tomber, glisser.

check.solution: **J'ai mal au dos.** *Le dos* is masculine, so *à + le* becomes **au**.

steps.title: Going deeper: when the participle does not agree
steps.body:
This is the rule that separates the top grades in this topic, and it looks like an exception until you see why.

With a reflexive verb, the past participle agrees with the reflexive pronoun **only when that pronoun is the direct object**.

Compare:

- *Elle s'est blessé**e***. — she injured *herself*. **Se** is the direct object, so it agrees.
- *Elle s'est blessé **la main***. — she injured *her hand*. The direct object is **la main**, which comes after the verb, so **no agreement**.

The same with breaking a bone:

- *Je me suis cassé **le bras***. — no agreement, even for a girl, because **le bras** is the direct object.

So the test is simple: **is there a noun straight after the participle?** If yes, no agreement. If no, agree with the subject.

*Se faire mal* never agrees either — *elle s'est **fait** mal* — because in *faire mal à quelqu'un* the reflexive pronoun is an **indirect** object, and only a direct object triggers agreement.

And the other grade 9 habit: mix your tenses. Use the **imperfect** for description and the **perfect** for events. *Je **faisais** du vélo quand je **suis tombé*** — I *was cycling* when I *fell*. That one sentence shows two past tenses and is worth more than a paragraph of either alone.

rows: la main is the direct object
Je me suis cassé le bras
props.title: The one test: is there a noun after the participle?

visuals.alt: A table contrasting reflexive perfect sentences that agree with those that do not

visuals.problem: Imperfect for the background, perfect for the event

steps.text: *Je **faisais** du vélo* — I was cycling: the background, so imperfect
*quand je **suis tombé*** — when I fell: a single event, so perfect
*Je faisais du vélo quand je suis tombé et je me suis cassé le bras.*
steps.note: Two past tenses in one sentence, and no agreement on cassé

steps.text: Add the near future and you have three: *Maintenant je **vais me reposer**.*

check.solution: No agreement, because **la cheville** is the direct object and follows the participle. The auxiliary is **être**, and the pronoun **s'** stays.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **avoir mal à** + body part, with the article contracted: **au** dos, **à la** tête, **à l'** estomac, **aux** dents. Learn each part with its article.
- **être malade**, but **avoir** un rhume / la grippe / **de la** fièvre.
- **Une ordonnance** is a prescription and **grave** means serious: two false friends the reading paper likes.
- **Every reflexive verb takes être in the perfect**: subject, pronoun, être, participle. *Je me suis couché*, *elle s'est blessée*.
- The participle **agrees with the subject** — unless a noun follows it. *Elle s'est blessée* agrees; *elle s'est blessé la main* does not.
- **Je me suis cassé le bras**: no agreement, and French says **le** bras, not *mon* bras.
- **Tomber** takes être and agrees; **glisser** takes avoir.
- **Depuis** + present means *have been*: *j'ai mal depuis deux jours* is *I have had it for two days*.
- **Imperfect for the background, perfect for the event**: *je faisais du vélo quand je suis tombé*.

je faisais du vélo quand je suis tombé

questions.solution: **Every** reflexive verb takes **être** in the perfect, without exception: *je me suis couché*, *elle s'est blessée*.

questions.prompt: Vous avez eu un accident. Écrivez environ 60 mots en français. Décrivez ce qui s'est passé, comment vous vous êtes senti, et ce que vous allez faire maintenant.
questions.solution: Level-marked on content and language. Three bullets, so three short paragraphs. The language marks come from using the perfect for what happened, an opinion or feeling, and the near future for what comes next, with reflexive verbs handled correctly throughout.

How you felt, with an opinion phrase or se sentir
What you are going to do, in the near future
Accurate auxiliaries and agreements, and a range of connectives rather than repeated et

questions.modelAnswer: Samedi dernier, je faisais du vélo avec mes amis quand je suis tombé dans la rue. Je me suis cassé le bras et je me suis fait mal à la cheville. Sur le moment, je me suis senti très inquiet, parce que ça faisait vraiment mal. Ma mère m'a emmené aux urgences et le médecin m'a donné une ordonnance. Maintenant, je vais me reposer pendant trois semaines et je ne vais pas faire de sport.

questions.prompt: Traduisez en français: *Last week I was ill. I had a temperature and a sore throat, so I went to the chemist's. The doctor gave me a prescription.*
questions.solution: **La semaine dernière, j'étais malade. J'avais de la fièvre et mal à la gorge, donc je suis allé à la pharmacie. Le médecin m'a donné une ordonnance.** The traps: *was ill* and *had* are descriptions, so they take the **imperfect** (*j'étais*, *j'avais*), not the perfect; *aller* takes **être**; and *gave me* puts the pronoun before the verb — *m'a donné*.

examTechnique.body:
This topic carries the grammar that the rest of Year 10 builds on: the perfect tense of reflexive verbs. Get the auxiliary right first — every reflexive verb takes **être**, with no list to learn — then the agreement, which is where the top marks are.

In the reading and listening papers, the traps are the false friends (*une ordonnance*, *grave*) and **depuis** + present, which English renders as a past. In writing and speaking, the fastest way to show range is the imperfect against the perfect: describe the background in one and the event in the other.

**Accents matter.** The app accepts an answer typed without them so a keyboard does not block you, but every solution shows the accented spelling, and the exam expects it.
examinerErrors: Using *avoir* with a reflexive verb: *j'ai me couché*. Every reflexive takes **être** in the perfect.
Writing *à le* or *à les*. They always contract to **au** and **aux**.
Agreeing the participle when a noun follows it: *je me suis cassée le bras*. The direct object is **le bras**, so there is no agreement.
Forgetting to agree when nothing follows: *elle s'est blessé* should be *elle s'est blessée*.
Saying *mon bras* after a reflexive: French uses **le bras**, because the pronoun already says whose it is.
Reading *une ordonnance* as an order, or *grave* as grave. Both are false friends.
Translating *depuis* + present as a plain present. *J'ai mal depuis deux jours* is *I have had it for two days*.
Staying in the perfect throughout a written answer. The imperfect for description, alongside the perfect for events, is what shows range.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer sets the scene in the imperfect and tells the event in the perfect, in the same sentence, and adds the near future for what happens next. Its reflexive verbs take être without hesitation, and it agrees the participle only when nothing follows it, so *elle s'est blessée* and *elle s'est blessé la main* both come out right. It uses the article rather than a possessive after a reflexive, handles **depuis** with the present, and gives reasons rather than listing symptoms.
